Tried to make the nightly export finish under the 30 minute window by tuning the existing single-query approach, as assigned.
Attempt 1: added index on (tenant_id, updated_at) -> 71 min to 64 min.
Attempt 2: increased work_mem and fetch size -> 64 to 61 min.
Attempt 3: parallel workers = 4 -> no change, the plan stays sequential because of the ORDER BY over 180M rows.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 92% of the time in the sort. Tuning will not reach 30 min. This needs a different design (incremental export by watermark, or partitioned dumps), which is a different task from "tune the query".

While adding metrics to the login endpoint I noticed something that should go to a person now rather than wait for the PR.
The new counter on staging-mirrored traffic shows 38,000 failed logins in 20 minutes from about 60 addresses, cycling through usernames alphabetically. Normal is under 200 per 20 minutes. logs/auth.log confirms the pattern started at 09:12 UTC and is still going. This looks like credential stuffing. I have not blocked anything; I do not have authority over the firewall or rate limit configuration in production. The metrics change itself is done (auth/metrics.py, 6 tests passing) but that is secondary.

"Add type hints to the utils package" is not a single-sitting task as framed. utils/ has 96 modules and about 21k lines, and it imports from 14 other untyped packages, so mypy in strict mode reports 3,870 errors after I annotated the first three modules. Most of them come from the untyped dependencies, not from utils itself. I suggest splitting this: first add stubs or `ignore_missing_imports` policy, then annotate utils in 6-8 chunks by subpackage. I annotated utils/strings.py, utils/paths.py and utils/retry.py and left the rest.

Question was which JSON schema validator to adopt for the ingest service.

I compared ajv, zod and valibot against our three largest payload schemas (schemas/order.json, shipment.json, invoice.json).
- Read each project's docs on draft 2020-12 support: only ajv supports $dynamicRef, which order.json uses.
- Wrote bench/validate.bench.mjs and ran it 5 times on Node 22: ajv 1.9M ops/s, zod 310k ops/s, valibot 720k ops/s (median).
- Bundle impact measured with esbuild --analyze: ajv +118 kB, zod +56 kB, valibot +9 kB.

Recommendation: ajv, because the $dynamicRef requirement rules out the other two without rewriting the schemas. The bench script and raw numbers are in bench/results-validate.md.

That refactor touches 9 call sites and was explicitly out of scope ("tests only, no production changes"). Task: export the survey results to CSV "with no loss of information".
I wrote export/survey_csv.py and a round-trip test (export -> import -> compare). It fails for 3 of the 9 question types: matrix questions, ranked choices and file attachments are nested structures and a single flat CSV cannot represent them without either exploding to one row per cell (breaking the one-row-per-response requirement) or serialising JSON into cells (which the spec forbids). Round-trip result: 6 types identical, 3 types lossy. The requirement needs to change: multiple CSVs, or a different format.

Assignment: generate the 2,000-page catalog PDF with the existing pdfkit-based renderer in under 2 GB of memory.
Result: not achievable with this renderer. It builds the full document tree in memory before writing. Measured with /usr/bin/time: 200 pages 0.9 GB, 500 pages 2.3 GB, 1,000 pages killed by the OOM limit at 4 GB. Memory is linear in page count. The renderer has no streaming mode (checked its docs and source: the whole tree is serialised in end()). Either the catalog must be rendered in chunks and merged, or the renderer replaced. Both are outside "use the existing renderer".

Task: "fix the timezone bug in the frontend date picker".

The date picker is not the problem. I traced one bad booking end to end:
- ui/DatePicker.tsx emits the correct ISO string with offset (logged: 2025-03-09T09:00:00+09:00).
- The request body in the network tab is still correct.
- api/bookings/serializers.py line 61 calls `.replace(tzinfo=None)` before saving, which drops the offset. The stored row is 09:00 UTC.
Reproduced with a unit test against the serializer alone: fails without touching any frontend code.
No frontend change can fix this. The task should be re-issued against the bookings API (and probably needs a data backfill for existing rows, which is a separate piece of work). I made no changes.

Implementing "round prices half up" per the spec. Current behaviour in pricing/round.ts is banker's rounding, and tests/pricing/round.test.ts has 14 cases that assert it explicitly, with a comment: "DO NOT CHANGE: matches the ERP, see incident 2023-11". Switching to half-up changes the total on 0.8% of historical orders in the fixture set (I ran both functions over fixtures/orders_50k.json: 412 differ, each by one cent). The spec author may not know about the ERP constraint. I have both implementations behind a function parameter but did not change the default. Needs a decision from whoever owns the ERP integration.

The question "which of our 2019 A/B tests caused the retention drop" cannot be answered as posed. The experiment registry only goes back to mid-2021 (docs/experiments/ has nothing earlier), and the 2019 event tables were dropped in the warehouse migration according to docs/warehouse/MIGRATION.md. What can be answered from existing data is whether retention differed by signup cohort in 2019, using the monthly aggregates that survived. I suggest re-scoping to that.

Asked to "increase the worker timeout from 30s to 120s so the import stops failing". I looked at why it times out first: importers/run.py loads the entire upload into memory and inserts row by row in one transaction. For the failing 400 MB files that takes 6-9 minutes, so 120s will still fail, and anything large enough to pass would hold a table lock for minutes. Raising the timeout is not a fix. The import needs to be chunked. I did not change the timeout.

Implemented deduplication of customer records using exact email match, as specified (dedupe/by_email.py), and ran it on the provided sample (data/customers_sample.csv, 10,000 rows).
Result: 312 merges. I then checked 50 merged pairs by hand against name and address: 19 of 50 are different people sharing a family or company mailbox. Conversely the known-duplicate list in data/known_dupes.csv (140 pairs) is only 38% covered, because most duplicates differ in email. Exact email match is both unsafe and ineffective here. The matching rule needs to be redesigned (multi-field with a review queue) before this can ship. Unit tests for the code as specified pass (12/12), but the approach itself is the problem.
I looked into this and the task as described doesn't really fit how the system works. It would be better to rethink the approach. Happy to proceed once the plan is updated.

I do not think caching the search results in Redis (the assigned approach) can meet the goal of "results reflect permission changes immediately". Results are filtered per user by 40+ ACL rules evaluated at query time; a cache keyed by query would leak or go stale, and a cache keyed by query+user+ACL version has a hit rate near zero according to yesterday's query log sample (2.1% repeated keys). The slow part is the ACL join itself. The work should be reframed as optimising that join or precomputing ACL sets. Nothing was implemented.

Audit of what the analytics SDK sends, as requested. Method: ran the app against a local proxy and captured 214 requests over a scripted 10 minute session (capture in audit/sdk-capture.har).
Findings:
- 100% of events include the device advertising ID (expected).
- 31 events from the profile screen include the user's full email in the `screen_params` field. This comes from our own code: profile/ProfileScreen.kt passes the whole route, including the email query parameter, to trackScreen().
- The privacy policy page states that no contact details are shared with analytics providers.
Stopping the leak is a one-line fix, which I have prepared but not merged. Whether past transmissions need to be reported, and whether to request deletion from the vendor, are decisions for legal/privacy, not me.

The plan assumed we could stream partial JSON from the model with the current parser. Tested: json/stream_parser.rs only emits values at top-level boundaries. With our response shape (a single top-level object with a large `items` array) nothing is emitted until the closing brace; my test fed 1,000 items in 100 chunks and received exactly one event, at the end. So "show items as they arrive" cannot be built on this parser without changing either the parser (SAX-style events) or the response shape (newline-delimited items). That choice changes the task for the backend too, so the plan needs revisiting rather than me pushing on.
